evals.prompt: Show me how to structure a TypeScript skill that has multiple actions. I want to build a skill with setup, run, and teardown modes.
evals.expected_output: Claude loads the example-typescript skill and explains Pattern B: SKILL.md frontmatter with execute pointing to scripts/run.sh --action=default, the action-based CLI pattern (--action=default, --action=random, --action=env), Bun runtime requirement, src/ for TypeScript source, and package.json for dependencies.

assertions.name: shows-action-based-cli-pattern
assertions.description: Response explains the --action= flag pattern that enables multiple modes in a single skill. Shows how execute field passes --action=default and how other actions can be invoked manually.

assertions.name: identifies-bun-runtime
assertions.description: Response specifies Bun as the runtime (not Node.js) and mentions the install command (brew install oven-sh/bun/bun).

assertions.name: shows-full-directory-anatomy
assertions.description: Response describes the complete skill structure: SKILL.md, scripts/run.sh (shell wrapper), src/ (TypeScript source), package.json (dependencies).

assertions.name: explains-pattern-b-use-cases
assertions.description: Response lists when to choose Pattern B: complex business logic, type safety, API calls, async operations, structured data, npm ecosystem.

assertions.name: contrasts-with-pattern-a
assertions.description: Response references Pattern A (example-bash) as the simpler alternative and explains why Pattern B is appropriate for multi-action skills.

evals.prompt: Just run the typescript example skill, I want to see what it outputs. Don't explain anything.
evals.expected_output: Claude runs scripts/run.sh --action=default and shows the output. But since this is a template/example skill, it still frames the output as a demonstration of the pattern, noting the action being executed and runtime info are part of the demo.

assertions.name: executes-via-scripts-run-sh
assertions.description: Claude runs the skill through scripts/run.sh (the shell wrapper), not by directly invoking bun or the TypeScript file. The execute field in frontmatter defines the entry point.

assertions.name: uses-default-action
assertions.description: The execution uses --action=default as specified in the frontmatter execute field, not a random or custom action.

assertions.name: preserves-educational-framing
assertions.description: Even when asked not to explain, the output itself demonstrates the pattern (showing action name, runtime info, structured data). Claude recognizes this IS the skill's purpose.

evals.prompt: I want to create a simple skill that just echoes 'hello world'. Should I use the TypeScript template? I also want it to work without installing anything.
evals.expected_output: Claude redirects to Pattern A (example-bash) since: no dependencies needed, simple linear logic, no structured data processing. TypeScript pattern requires Bun runtime installation, which violates the 'no install' requirement. A bash skill with echo is the simplest possible implementation.

assertions.name: redirects-to-bash-pattern
assertions.description: Claude recommends example-bash (Pattern A) over example-typescript (Pattern B) for a simple echo skill. Over-engineering with TypeScript for trivial tasks is an anti-pattern.

assertions.name: flags-bun-dependency
assertions.description: Response identifies that TypeScript pattern requires Bun runtime to be installed, which conflicts with the user's 'no install' constraint.

assertions.name: explains-pattern-selection-honestly
assertions.description: Claude does not try to make the TypeScript template work for this case. The skill has clear criteria for when each pattern applies and Claude follows them.
